# Building the Platinum Bridge

The bridge is an ESP32 board between your classic Mac and your computer. Depending on what you wire up it can:

- **Be the Mac's keyboard and mouse** — an ADB keyboard + mouse (Macintosh SE and later) or an M0110 keyboard + quadrature mouse (128K, 512K, Plus). Type from Platinum, or pair any Bluetooth LE keyboard and mouse with the bridge.
- **Carry the Mac's serial port over WiFi, USB or Bluetooth** — this is what Platinum Agent uses for file transfer, the remote screen and the debugger.
- **Power the Mac on** from the app (ADB machines with a soft-power key: Mac II, LC, Quadra…).

The **Hardware & link** page in Platinum draws this same wiring interactively for your exact Mac and board. This document is the printable version.

> [!WARNING]
> Classic Macs are 30+ years old and their parts are irreplaceable. Check every pin of every cable with a multimeter before plugging it in, never connect +12 V to anything, and keep the ESP32's 3.3 V logic away from the Mac's 5 V lines — always go through the level shifter or transceiver listed here.

## Pick a board

| Board | Chip | Bluetooth | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **ESP32-S3-DevKitC-1** | ESP32-S3 (Xtensa LX7 dual-core, 240 MHz) | Bluetooth LE 5 (BLE keyboards and mice) | Recommended: native USB, more RAM and the LCD_CAM peripheral for future video capture. |
| **ESP32-DevKitC (WROOM-32)** | ESP32 (Xtensa LX6 dual-core, 240 MHz) | Bluetooth Classic + LE 4.2 | The most common and cheapest. GPIO 34–39 are input-only. |

### Pin map

The firmware uses these GPIOs (see `firmware/platinum-bridge/config.h`).

| Signal | ESP32-S3-DevKitC-1 | ESP32-DevKitC (WROOM-32) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `ADB_DATA` | GPIO 4 | GPIO 25 |
| `ADB_PSW` | GPIO 5 | GPIO 26 |
| `SER_TX` | GPIO 17 | GPIO 17 |
| `SER_RX` | GPIO 18 | GPIO 16 |
| `KBD_CLK` | GPIO 10 | GPIO 32 |
| `KBD_DATA` | GPIO 11 | GPIO 33 |
| `MOUSE_X1` | GPIO 12 | GPIO 21 |
| `MOUSE_X2` | GPIO 13 | GPIO 22 |
| `MOUSE_Y1` | GPIO 14 | GPIO 23 |
| `MOUSE_Y2` | GPIO 15 | GPIO 27 |
| `MOUSE_SW` | GPIO 16 | GPIO 13 |
| `LED` | GPIO 48 | GPIO 2 |

## Wiring by Mac family

Each family below shows the ESP32-S3 wiring with keyboard/mouse and the serial port enabled, powered over USB. For the classic ESP32 swap the GPIO numbers using the pin map above.

### Macintosh 128K and 512K

M0110 keyboard, quadrature mouse and a DE-9 serial port.

Applies to: Macintosh 128K, Macintosh 512K.

**Connections**

| Signal | ESP32-S3 | Through | Mac |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Mouse X1 | GPIO12 | 74AHCT125 1A→1Y | DE-9 pin 5 |
| Mouse X2 | GPIO13 | 74AHCT125 2A→2Y | DE-9 pin 4 |
| Mouse Y1 | GPIO14 | 74AHCT125 3A→3Y | DE-9 pin 9 |
| Mouse Y2 | GPIO15 | 74AHCT125 4A→4Y | DE-9 pin 8 |
| Keyboard CLK | GPIO10 | BSS138 LV1→HV1 | RJ-11 pin 2 |
| Keyboard DATA | GPIO11 | BSS138 LV2→HV2 | RJ-11 pin 3 |
| Mouse button | GPIO16 | BSS138 LV3→HV3 | DE-9 pin 7 |
| +5 V / GND | 3V3 / GND | BSS138 HV/GND | RJ-11 4 / 1, DE-9 2 / 3 |
| ESP32 → Mac | GPIO17 | MAX3488 DI → Y/Z | RxD+ (8) / RxD− (9) |
| Mac → ESP32 | GPIO18 | MAX3488 A/B → RO | TxD+ (4) / TxD− (5) |
| Ground | GND | common | GND (3) |

**Parts**

| Qty | Part | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | ESP32-S3-DevKitC-1 | The bridge: WiFi, Bluetooth and USB |
| 1 | BSS138 level shifter (4-channel) | Keyboard (CLK, DATA) and mouse button at 5 V |
| 1 | 74AHCT125 (or 74HCT125) | Clean 5 V quadrature outputs |
| 1 | RJ-11 4P4C phone cable | Keyboard port |
| 1 | Male DE-9 connector | Mouse port |
| 1 | MAX3488 (or SN65HVD379 / a 3.3 V RS-422 module) | The Mac's serial port is differential RS-422 |
| 1 | Male DE-9 connector | Modem/Printer port |
| 1 | 100 nF capacitor | MAX3488 decoupling |

**Before you plug in**

- Use the Modem port for the agent. If AppleTalk is on, the Printer port may be busy.
- USB power: still connect the ESP32's ground (GND) to the Mac's.
- Check every pin of the cable for continuity with a multimeter before plugging it into the Mac. Connector diagrams show the front of the Mac's port.

### ADB Macs (SE, II, Classic, LC, Quadra, Power Macintosh…)

ADB for keyboard and mouse and the mini-DIN-8 serial port. Shown for the Macintosh SE; every ADB model is wired the same way.

Applies to: Macintosh SE, Macintosh II, Macintosh SE/30, Macintosh IIcx, Macintosh Classic, Macintosh LC, Macintosh IIci, Macintosh IIfx, Macintosh Classic II, Quadra 650, Quadra 800, Power Macintosh 6100, Power Macintosh 7500, Power Macintosh 9500, Power Macintosh G3 (Beige).

**Connections**

| Signal | ESP32-S3 | Through | Mac |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| ADB data | GPIO4 | BSS138 LV1→HV1 | ADB pin 1 |
| Power-on (PSW) | GPIO5 | 2N7000 (drain) | ADB pin 2 |
| +5 V reference | — | BSS138 HV | ADB pin 3 |
| Ground | GND | common | ADB pin 4 |
| ESP32 → Mac | GPIO17 | MAX3488 DI → Y/Z | RxD+ (8) / RxD− (5) |
| Mac → ESP32 | GPIO18 | MAX3488 A/B → RO | TxD+ (6) / TxD− (3) |
| Ground | GND | common | GND (4) |

**Parts**

| Qty | Part | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | ESP32-S3-DevKitC-1 | The bridge: WiFi, Bluetooth and USB |
| 1 | BSS138 level shifter (4-channel) | The ADB line is 5 V and the ESP32 can't take that |
| 1 | 2N7000 MOSFET + 1 kΩ resistor | Power the Mac on from the app (Power key) |
| 1 | Male mini-DIN-4 cable/connector (S-Video works) | Connects to the ADB port |
| 1 | MAX3488 (or SN65HVD379 / a 3.3 V RS-422 module) | The Mac's serial port is differential RS-422 |
| 1 | Male mini-DIN-8 cable (Mac printer cable) | Modem/Printer port |
| 1 | 100 nF capacitor | MAX3488 decoupling |

**Before you plug in**

- On compact Macs (SE, Classic) the PSW pin doesn't power the machine on: use the switch on the back.
- Use the Modem port for the agent. If AppleTalk is on, the Printer port may be busy.
- USB power: still connect the ESP32's ground (GND) to the Mac's.
- Check every pin of the cable for continuity with a multimeter before plugging it into the Mac. Connector diagrams show the front of the Mac's port.

### Powering the bridge from the Mac

On ADB Macs the bridge can run from the ADB port's +5 V instead of USB (toggle **Mac power** in the app). The whole ADB bus has 500 mA, and the ESP32's WiFi draws spikes, so add a 470 µF / 10 V electrolytic capacitor across +5 V and GND and keep other ADB devices to a minimum. On the Mac Plus and earlier, power the bridge over USB.

## Connector pinouts

All drawings in Platinum show the **front of the socket on the Mac**, looking into it.

### ADB (mini-DIN-4)

Apple Desktop Bus. Open-collector data line with a 5 V pull-up inside the Mac. +5 V is limited to 500 mA for the whole bus.

| Pin | Name | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | `ADB` | ADB data (bidirectional, 5 V, open collector) |
| 2 | `PSW` | Power-on: pull to GND to switch on (Mac II, LC, Quadra…) |
| 3 | `+5V` | Power (max. 500 mA for the whole bus) |
| 4 | `GND` | Ground |

### Modem/Printer serial port (mini-DIN-8)

Differential RS-422 (Zilog 8530 SCC). Up to 57.6 kbps as standard; 230.4 kbps with an external clock on HSKi. Pin 7 (GPi) doesn't exist on the Mac Plus.

| Pin | Name | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | `HSKo` | Handshake out (DTR) |
| 2 | `HSKi` | Handshake in / external clock |
| 3 | `TxD−` | Transmit − |
| 4 | `GND` | Ground |
| 5 | `RxD−` | Receive − |
| 6 | `TxD+` | Transmit + |
| 7 | `GPi` | General-purpose input (not on the Mac Plus) |
| 8 | `RxD+` | Receive + |

### Serial port (DE-9, Mac 128K/512K)

RS-422 on a DE-9. Pins 2 (+5 V) and 6 (+12 V) carry power: don't short them.

| Pin | Name | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | `GND` | Ground (chassis) |
| 2 | `+5V` | +5 V |
| 3 | `GND` | Ground |
| 4 | `TxD+` | Transmit + |
| 5 | `TxD−` | Transmit − |
| 6 | `+12V` | +12 V — do not connect |
| 7 | `HSK` | Handshake / external clock |
| 8 | `RxD+` | Receive + |
| 9 | `RxD−` | Receive − |

### Keyboard (RJ-11 4P4C, Mac 128K/512K/Plus)

Synchronous M0110 protocol: the keyboard generates the clock and the Mac polls it every ~250 ms.

| Pin | Name | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | `GND` | Ground |
| 2 | `CLK` | Clock (driven by the keyboard) |
| 3 | `DATA` | Bidirectional data |
| 4 | `+5V` | +5 V |

### Mouse (DE-9, Mac 128K/512K/Plus)

Quadrature mouse: two phase-shifted signals per axis (X1/X2, Y1/Y2) and an active-low button.

| Pin | Name | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | `GND` | Ground |
| 2 | `+5V` | +5 V |
| 3 | `GND` | Ground |
| 4 | `X2` | X quadrature, phase 2 |
| 5 | `X1` | X quadrature, phase 1 |
| 6 | `NC` | Not connected |
| 7 | `SW` | Button (active low) |
| 8 | `Y2` | Y quadrature, phase 2 |
| 9 | `Y1` | Y quadrature, phase 1 |

## Flashing the firmware

The firmware is an Arduino sketch in `firmware/platinum-bridge/`. Platinum's **Hardware & link → Firmware** tab runs these commands for you; by hand they are:

```sh
arduino-cli core install esp32:esp32
arduino-cli lib install "NimBLE-Arduino" "WebSockets" "ArduinoJson"

# ESP32-S3-DevKitC-1
arduino-cli compile --fqbn esp32:esp32:esp32s3:CDCOnBoot=cdc firmware/platinum-bridge
arduino-cli upload -p <port> --fqbn esp32:esp32:esp32s3:CDCOnBoot=cdc firmware/platinum-bridge
# ESP32-DevKitC (WROOM-32)
arduino-cli compile --fqbn esp32:esp32:esp32 firmware/platinum-bridge
arduino-cli upload -p <port> --fqbn esp32:esp32:esp32 firmware/platinum-bridge
```

`<port>` is `COM5` or similar on Windows, `/dev/cu.usbmodem…` on macOS and `/dev/ttyACM0` on Linux. If an ESP32-S3 isn't detected the first time, hold **BOOT**, tap **RST** and release **BOOT**.

With no WiFi configured the bridge starts an access point called `Platinum-XXXX` (password `macintosh`) at 192.168.4.1. Send it your network's credentials from **Hardware & link → Bridge & network**; after a restart it shows up as `platinum.local`.

## First power-on checklist

1. Mac **off**. Bridge connected to your computer over USB only.
2. Flash the firmware and connect from Platinum over USB. The bridge log should say `Platinum Bridge v… ready`.
3. Check continuity of every wire against the tables above, and that nothing touches +12 V.
4. Plug the bridge into the Mac and switch the Mac on.
5. On **Keyboard & mouse**, the bus monitor should show the Mac polling the bridge within a couple of seconds. If it doesn't, re-check the data line and the level shifter's HV/LV supply.
6. Click the remote-control area and move the mouse: the Mac's pointer should follow.
